You are a research agent that fact-checks claims made in podcasts, interviews, and articles. Use the web_search tool to find evidence.

## What you get
A verbatim excerpt highlighted from a podcast, interview, or article — the specific claim to check — plus the surrounding passage for context. The message shows them as:
  Highlighted claim from Transcript: <verbatim excerpt>   (or "Highlighted claim from Article:")
  Surrounding context: <surrounding passage>
Some claims rest on an image instead of (or in addition to) text. A claim with no highlighted text comes from an image; since one image can carry several claims, a "Claim: <restatement>" line then names the one to check — judge only that claim against the described image. Judge whether the claim is factually correct.

## Output format
Return JSON with two fields:
- findings: a dense research summary. Include the full https:// source URL inline next to each claim it supports — write out the complete link, never use footnote numbers, domain shortcuts, or citation markers.
- correction_needed: true only if the claim contains a clear factual error supported by direct contradicting evidence.

## When NOT to set correction_needed = true
- Opinions, predictions, or subjective characterizations
- Claims that are factually correct, or approximations that are directionally right
- When you can't find strong contradicting evidence

## Sourcing rules
- Include what each source says that's relevant.
- If no correction is needed, the findings can be brief — just explain why.

Respond with strict JSON only matching: { findings: string, correction_needed: boolean }

content.findings:
The claim that India's open defecation (OD) rate 'remains high, at around 28%' is not supported by any current data source; 28% corresponds roughly to India's national OD rate around 2015.

1) WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP), the standard international source: <cite index="4-4">According to WHO's latest data (2022), 11% of India's population practises open defecation</cite> (https://newschecker.in/fact-check/india-tops-in-open-defecation-no-heres-the-truth-behind-viral-infographic; corroborated at https://dfrac.org/en/2025/01/04/fact-checking-the-viral-infographic-on-open-defecation/ — <cite index="7-10">India's open-defecation rate stands at 11% (WHO's latest data, 2022)</cite>). Rural-only figures are higher but still well under 28%: <cite index="1-1">in 2015 some 41% of India's rural population defecated in the open, versus 17% in 2022</cite> (https://www.downtoearth.org.in/water/is-open-defecation-back-in-india--90483); <cite index="12-1,12-2">World Bank/JMP data put rural OD at 17.0% in 2022, down from 20.4% in 2021</cite> (https://www.ceicdata.com/en/india/social-access-to-services/people-practicing-open-defecation-rural--of-rural-population).

2) Latest World Bank/JMP series: <cite index="10-1">people practicing open defecation in India was 6.73% of population in 2024</cite> and <cite index="11-1">10.66% of the rural population in 2024</cite> (https://tradingeconomics.com/india/people-practicing-open-defecation-percent-of-population-wb-data.html, https://tradingeconomics.com/india/people-practicing-open-defecation-rural-percent-of-rural-population-wb-data.html; underlying source https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.STA.ODFC.ZS?locations=IN).

3) Indian survey data, which tend to be less flattering than administrative data, still fall short of 28%: <cite index="23-3,23-7">NFHS-5 (2019-21) found households practicing open defecation fell from 39% in 2015-16 to 19%, with 19% of households having no facility</cite> (https://pragnews.com/en/nfhs-survey-19-of-homes-have-no-toilet-facility-in-bihar; also https://www.researchgate.net/publication/384535883 — <cite index="21-1">19.4% of households had no toilet facility in 2019-21</cite>). More recent: <cite index="24-6,24-7">an analysis of the 2022-23 Household Consumption Expenditure Survey found 12.5% of Indian households have no toilet, about 162 million people</cite> (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12180355). Data For India notes <cite index="22-11,22-12">OD fell from 70% in 1993 to 19% by 2021, though about one in four rural households still do not use a toilet</cite> (https://www.dataforindia.com/sanitation/) — i.e. ~25% is a rural, not national, figure and is from 2021.

4) For historical calibration: <cite index="6-12">JMP data show that by 2015, 57% of Indians had a toilet while 29% were defecating in the open</cite> (https://jogh.org/2023/jogh-13-04082) — matching the ~28% figure to the pre-/early-Swachh Bharat period, not the present.

Conclusion: the ~28% figure is roughly a decade out of date. Current national OD estimates are about 7-11% (JMP/World Bank), with survey-based no-toilet/OD estimates of 12.5-19%; rural-only estimates are ~17% (2022) to ~25% (2021 non-use). Commenters noting the number is lower today are correct. The article's broader point (open defecation persists despite toilet construction, with usage/behaviour lagging) is directionally valid, but the specific 28% figure is a clear factual error.

You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. The downstream judge will record "no_correction_needed" and we move on. This is correct behavior when no evidence-supported dispute is available.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

## The time-travel test
The post context states when the post was published. A post is not wrong for failing to know the future: if your correction relies on facts that only became true after the post was published (a later goal, a completed transfer, an updated figure), the post has not made a correctable error. If your note would not have been accurate and fair at the moment the post was published, return an empty note.

## Research findings

### 28% OD figure is outdated
The claim that India's open defecation (OD) rate 'remains high, at around 28%' is not supported by any current data source. That figure corresponds roughly to India's national OD rate around 2015 (JMP data show that by 2015, 57% of Indians had a toilet while 29% were defecating in the open, per https://jogh.org/2023/jogh-13-04082), not the present day. Current WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) data show India's open-defecation rate at 11% in 2022 (https://newschecker.in/fact-check/india-tops-in-open-defecation-no-heres-the-truth-behind-viral-infographic, corroborated at https://dfrac.org/en/2025/01/04/fact-checking-the-viral-infographic-on-open-defecation/). The latest World Bank/JMP series puts it even lower: 6.73% of the population in 2024 nationally, and 10.66% of the rural population in 2024 (https://tradingeconomics.com/india/people-practicing-open-defecation-percent-of-population-wb-data.html, https://tradingeconomics.com/india/people-practicing-open-defecation-rural-percent-of-rural-population-wb-data.html; underlying source https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.STA.ODFC.ZS?locations=IN). content.findings:
The claim that ~35% of UP children attend private schools is well below every major data source.

Administrative data (UDISE+): A UP-specific analysis of UDISE+ finds private unaided schools' share of state enrolment "rising from 44.27% in 2021-22 to 50.12% in 2024-25" (https://educationforallinindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/School-Education-in-Uttar-Pradesh-Where-do-we-stand-UDISEPlus-2021-22-to-2024-25.pdf). FACTLY's summary of UDISE+ 2025-26 reports UP "crossed the halfway mark for private enrolment, with the private share rising from 42% to 54%," listing UP among states where private schools now enrol a majority (54%) (https://factly.in/public-school-enrolment-falls-as-private-schools-expand/). The same UDISE+ 2025-26 cycle shows UP with 23.1 million private-unaided students, the largest absolute private enrolment of any state, and places UP among northern-plains states at or above the national private share of ~40% (https://educationforallinindia.com/private-schools-cross-the-40-enrolment-mark-the-government-to-private-shift-in-udise-2025-26/).

Household-survey data (ASER, rural only): nationally, private enrolment for ages 6-14 in rural India is 33.2% in 2024, with government share at 66.8% (down from 72.9% in 2022 and roughly back to the 65.6% level of 2018) (https://ruralindiaonline.org/en/library/resource/annual-status-of-education-report-rural-2024/, https://www.ideasforindia.in/topics/human-development/aser-2024-more-than-a-post-pandemic-recovery-in-learning). That 33% is a rural-only, all-India figure; UP is consistently cited among states with rapid private expansion, and UP's private share (rural + urban) is higher than the rural national average. Even the household-based NSS Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education 2025 puts private unaided recognised schools at ~32% of enrolment nationwide, with government share only ~30% in urban areas (https://www.newsonair.gov.in/government-schools-account-for-56-of-enrolments-says-education-survey-2025, https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/one-third-school-students-take-private-coaching-trend-more-common-in-urban-areas-centres-survey) — again a national, not UP, figure, and UP sits above the national level.

One caveat: an educationforallinindia national piece contains a stray line describing UP as "39.8% [schools] → 14.6% enrolment" and itself calls that figure "anomalous" (https://educationforallinindia.com/role-of-private-and-government-aided-schools-in-indian-education-system-2024-25/); the same site's dedicated UP paper gives 50.12%, so the 14.6% appears to be an error.

On the author's caveat that higher figures reflect misreporting: no located source produces a ~35% figure for UP, and the known measurement bias runs the other way — UP audit findings document inflated government-school rolls and very low actual attendance (CAG found 27% attendance against enrolment in sampled schools; https://www.deccanherald.com/india/enrolments-up-govt-schools-decline-2005423), which would if anything understate the private share. Historical context also supports a large private sector in UP well before recent years (https://ideas.repec.org/h/spr/isbchp/978-981-13-6443-3_15.html).

Bottom line: UP's private-school share is roughly 50-54% on the latest UDISE+ data and around/above the ~33% rural national figure even on household surveys; "around 35%" understates it by roughly 15-19 percentage points.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)

  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."

- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair

- Target: 240-260 non-URL characters
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

Infrastructure gaps— including uneven access to electricity, digital tools, and specialised facilities—contribute to overcrowded classrooms and variable learning environments. Gender and regional disparities endure, with rural and eastern districts lagging behind urban and western ones. The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated these inequities by extending closures that impacted millions of learners. Samagra Shiksha (integrating Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan since 2018) has driven school construction, teacher recruitment, and access enhancements across UP's extensive network. An Analysis of UDISE+ 2021–22 to 2024–25 Data," presents a rigorous, evidence-based examination of the state's school system. Relying solely on official UDISE+ reports, it examines trends in school distribution (by level and management), enrolment patterns, gender parity, enrolment ratios (GER, NER), dropout and transition rates, retention, teacher availability and training, and essential facilities. It offers concluding observations on strengths and limitations, the feasibility of achieving universal education by 2030, and recommendations for optimising Samagra Shiksha. # Public School Enrolment Falls as Private Schools Expand

**TL;DR** India’s latest UDISE+ 2025–26 data reveals a school education system in transition. While government schools continue to educate the majority of students nationally, private schools are steadily gaining ground, particularly at the primary level and in several states. The report also highlights persistent gaps in early childhood education, with one in five children entering government schools without preschool experience. Together, these trends point to shifting parental preferences, changing enrolment patterns, and emerging policy challenges around school planning, teacher deployment, and foundational learning.

**Context**  
School education is often discussed through the lens of board exam results, budget announcements, or ambitious policy promises. Yet the quieter story lies in the data that captures who enters the classroom, who stays, where schools are expanding, and where the system continues to fall short. Released annually by the Ministry of Education, [UDISE+](https://udiseplus.gov.in/#/en/page/publications) is India’s most comprehensive administrative database on school education, offering a granular view of nearly every recognised school, teacher, and student across the country. The 2025–26 report arrives at a crucial moment, as governments seek to achieve the National Education Policy’s goals of universal participation and improved learning outcomes while confronting slowing demographic growth, uneven digital readiness, and persistent regional disparities. Beyond headline numbers, the data reveals how India’s schooling landscape is changing, highlighting shifts in enrolment, infrastructure, teacher deployment, equity, and access that will shape education policy in the years ahead.

In today’s story, we examine the report’s most important findings and what they reveal about the state of school education in India.

**Who compiles this data?**  
The data is compiled annually by the Department of School Education and Literacy (DoSE&L), Ministry of Education, through [the Unified District Information System for Education Plus (UDISE+)](https://udiseplus.gov.in/#/en/page/about). Schools upload data directly to the UDISE+ platform, where it undergoes multiple stages of verification at the block, district, and state levels before being consolidated into a national database, making it the government’s primary repository of school education statistics.

**Key Insights**

**Private schools now enrol the majority of students in several states**  
The balance between public and private schooling varies sharply across India, reflecting differences in income levels, urbanisation, and the historical strength of government school systems. Nationally, government and government-aided schools continue to educate the majority of students, accounting for 58% of total enrolment in 2025–26, compared with 40% in private schools. However, this lead has narrowed steadily from 65% versus 33% in 2022–23, underscoring the continued shift towards private schooling.

The trend is even more pronounced in several states. By 2025–26, private schools enrolled a majority of students in Haryana (62%), Telangana (65%), Nagaland (67%), Manipur (66%), Andhra Pradesh (57%), Uttar Pradesh (54%), Uttarakhand (62%), Punjab (53%), Rajasthan (53%), Puducherry (61%), Mizoram (51%) and Ladakh (53%), while Karnataka and Tamil Nadu were evenly split between government and private schools. In contrast, government schools continue to dominate enrolment in states such as West Bengal (87%), Goa (86%), Bihar (81%), Odisha (78%), Tripura (73%), Kerala (70%), Assam (69%) and Jharkhand (68%), where they remain the principal providers of school education.

Several states have also witnessed notable shifts over the past four years. Andhra Pradesh moved from a near-even split in 2022–23 (51% government, 49% private) to a clear private majority in 2025–26 (43% government, 57% private). Uttar Pradesh crossed the halfway mark for private enrolment, with the private share rising from 42% to 54%, while Haryana saw private schools increase their share from 55% to 62%. Telangana recorded one of the largest changes, with private enrolment rising from 56% to 65%, and Uttarakhand from 51% to 62%. By contrast, states such as West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Kerala and Goa have seen only marginal changes, with government schools continuing to enrol a large majority of students despite a gradual increase in the private share. These contrasting trajectories suggest that the shift towards private schooling is not uniform across India but is concentrated in a relatively small group of states where the expansion of private education has accelerated over the past decade, along with changing preferences.

**Public-Private enrolment gap at the Primary level shrinks by 54%**  
India’s school enrolment landscape has steadily shifted towards private institutions over the past four academic years. Between 2022–23 and 2025–26, enrolment in government and government-aided schools declined across almost every stage of schooling. The sharpest fall was at the primary level, where public schools lost over 1.53 crore students (21%), while elementary enrolment (Classes 1–8) declined by 1.93 crore students (16%). In contrast, private unaided schools recorded consistent growth, adding 51 lakh primary students (14%) and 88 lakh elementary students (16%) over the same period.

Although government schools continue to educate more children than private schools, the gap is narrowing rapidly. At the elementary level, the enrolment difference between government/government-aided and private unaided schools shrank from 6.33 crore students in 2022–23 to 3.53 crore in 2025–26, a reduction of 2.81 crore students (44%). The gap at the primary level more than halved, falling from 3.83 crore to 1.78 crore students. The trend is far less pronounced at the secondary and higher secondary levels, suggesting that the shift towards private schooling is strongest during the foundational years.

The trend carries important policy implications. Government schools remain the backbone of India’s education system, particularly in rural and disadvantaged regions. Falling enrolment affects teacher deployment, school consolidation, and infrastructure planning, while the growing preference for private schools raises important questions about parental perceptions of quality, affordability, and the future role of public education in delivering equitable access to schooling.

A child’s first day in Class 1 is not their first day of learning. Preschool helps build the language, social, cognitive, and motor skills that prepare children for formal schooling, which is why the [National Education Policy (NEP) 2020](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/NEP_Final_English_0.pdf) places Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) at the heart of the foundational stage.

The contrast underscores the central role of India’s public ECCE system in preparing children for government schools, while private schools largely rely on integrated preschool-to-primary pipelines.

UDISE+ is more than a statistical exercise; it provides the evidence that shapes education policy, public spending, and school planning across India. As the country moves from expanding access to improving quality under the National Education Policy 2020, understanding where students enrol, how they enter the school system, and which institutions they choose becomes increasingly important. The same UDISE+ 2025-26 cycle shows UP with 23.1 million private-unaided students, the largest absolute private enrolment of any state, and places UP among northern-plains states at or above the national private share of ~40% (https://educationforallinindia.com/private-schools-cross-the-40-enrolment-mark-the-government-to-private-shift-in-udise-2025-26/).

Household-survey data (ASER, rural only): nationally, private enrolment for ages 6-14 in rural India is 33.2% in 2024, with government share at 66.8% (down from 72.9% in 2022 and roughly back to the 65.6% level of 2018) (https://ruralindiaonline.org/en/library/resource/annual-status-of-education-report-rural-2024/, https://www.ideasforindia.in/topics/human-development/aser-2024-more-than-a-post-pandemic-recovery-in-learning). That 33% is a rural-only, all-India figure; UP is consistently cited among states with rapid private expansion, and UP's private share (rural + urban) is higher than the rural national average. Even the household-based NSS Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education 2025 puts private unaided recognised schools at ~32% of enrolment nationwide, with government share only ~30% in urban areas (https://www.newsonair.gov.in/government-schools-account-for-56-of-enrolments-says-education-survey-2025, https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/one-third-school-students-take-private-coaching-trend-more-common-in-urban-areas-centres-survey) — again a national, not UP, figure, and UP sits above the national level.

One caveat: an educationforallinindia national piece contains a stray line describing UP as "39.8% [schools] → 14.6% enrolment" and itself calls that figure "anomalous" (https://educationforallinindia.com/role-of-private-and-government-aided-schools-in-indian-education-system-2024-25/); the same site's dedicated UP paper gives 50.12%, so the 14.6% appears to be an error.

On the author's caveat that higher figures reflect misreporting: no located source produces a ~35% figure for UP, and the known measurement bias runs the other way — UP audit findings document inflated government-school rolls and very low actual attendance (CAG found 27% attendance against enrolment in sampled schools; https://www.deccanherald.com/india/enrolments-up-govt-schools-decline-2005423), which would if anything understate the private share. Historical context also supports a large private sector in UP well before recent years (https://ideas.repec.org/h/spr/isbchp/978-981-13-6443-3_15.html).

Bottom line: UP's private-school share is roughly 50-54% on the latest UDISE+ data and around/above the ~33% rural national figure even on household surveys; "around 35%" understates it by roughly 15-19 percentage points.

The claim invokes the Boserup/Goody "hoe vs. plough" thesis, which is a real and widely cited hypothesis in anthropology and economics, so it is not a fabrication.

Supporting evidence: Boserup (Woman's Role in Economic Development, 1970) argued bride price arises where light-tool (hoe/swidden) farming makes women's agricultural labor valuable, while dowry arises in plough societies where women contribute little to field work. <cite index="4-1">Boserup "has argued that bride-price is found in societies in which agriculture relies on light tools (such as the hoe) and where women are actively engaged and dowry is found in societies where heavier plough agriculture is practised and women have a limited role"</cite> (http://www.isid.ac.in/~epu/acegd2018/papers/DimpleKukreja.pdf). <cite index="1-12,1-13">Bride-price societies feature high female contribution to agricultural work (typically swidden), high female autonomy and more polygyny; dowry societies feature low female contribution (typically plough systems), dependence on husbands, and low polygyny</cite> (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229492793_Dowry_as_Female_Competition). Jack Goody made a parallel argument: <cite index="9-2,9-3">he demonstrated a historical correlation between "diverging devolution" (dowry) and intensive plough agriculture on one hand, and homogeneous inheritance (brideprice) and extensive hoe agriculture on the other, drawing on Boserup</cite> (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowry). Alesina, Giuliano & Nunn (QJE 2013) tested and largely confirmed the mechanism for gender norms: <cite index="31-5,31-6,31-7,31-8,31-9">Boserup's hypothesis is that gender-role differences originate in the traditional form of agriculture — shifting hoe/digging-stick cultivation vs. capital-intensive plough cultivation, the latter requiring upper-body strength and bursts of power</cite>, and <cite index="28-1">they find a strong, robust relationship between historical plough use and unequal gender roles today</cite> (https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/nunn/files/alesina_giuliano_nunn_qje_2013.pdf, https://igier.unibocconi.eu/sites/default/files/media/attach/Part_A.pdf). Plough societies are also linked to dowry and son preference (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0190510): <cite index="7-4,7-5,7-6">girls came to be valued less, producing dowry, while societies without the plough more likely developed bride price</cite>.

Caveats/nuance (why "fundamental cause" is an overstatement, especially as applied to post-marital residence): cross-cultural research on patrilocal vs. matrilocal residence does not identify agricultural technology as the primary driver. Ember & Ember (American Anthropologist 1971) found <cite index="23-3,23-4,23-5">that the traditional assumption that division of labor determines residence was not supported; instead patrilocality is favored by internal warfare and matrilocality by purely external warfare when women do at least as much subsistence work as men</cite> (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229796585_The_Conditions_Favoring_Matrilocal_Versus_Patrilocal_Residence). Goody's materialist argument is also contested — <cite index="15-9">Tambiah objected that in Eurasian/urban societies dowry appears at the top of the social ladder and bridewealth-like practices at the bottom, a class dimension the theory neglects</cite> (https://davidgraeber.org/videos/debt-service-and-the-origins-of-capitalism/), and <cite index="9-10">there is scholarly debate on Goody's theory</cite>. Alesina et al. themselves concede reverse causality is possible (<cite index="32-1,32-2">the same correlations would appear if societies with gender-unequal attitudes were more likely to adopt the plough</cite>). Competing explanations for bride price/dowry exist, e.g. the female-competition model, which <cite index="1-7,1-8">outperformed Boserup's labor-value model on 1,267 Ethnographic Atlas societies</cite>. Empirically, sub-Saharan Africa is overwhelmingly hoe-based yet predominantly patrilocal with bridewealth, so hoe agriculture does not by itself produce uxorilocal/matrilocal residence.

This is an interpretive/theoretical overstatement rather than a discrete factual error, so no correction is warranted.

Data come from emigration passes/repatriation records for Indians entering Fiji 1879–1916, restricted to north Indians departing Calcutta. The claim matches the paper's headline results. The paper is Emily Breza, Supreet Kaur, and Nandita Krishnaswamy, "Social Norms as a Determinant of Aggregate Labor Supply" (earlier circulated as "Scabs: The Social Suppression of Labor Supply"), NBER WP 25880 — listed on Supreet Kaur's site as "Accepted, Journal of Political Economy, 2026" (https://www.supreetkaur.com/research), so the "(2026)" citation year is appropriate.

Abstract figures (https://www.nber.org/papers/w25880 and https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3395641): "Only 1.8% of agricultural workers are willing to accept jobs below the prevailing wage despite high unemployment, but this number jumps to 26% when this choice is not observable to other workers" — i.e., <2% public vs. ~a quarter private, exactly as stated. Same wording in the working paper PDF (https://www.atai-research.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Unions.pdf).

Design details support the specifics: the field experiment used 183 employers offering jobs to 502 workers in informal spot labor markets in rural Odisha, India, with jobs offered either at the prevailing wage or 10% below it, and with randomized observability of the wage/acceptance (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0060356p, https://voxdev.org/topic/labour-markets/scabs-social-suppression-labour-supply, https://spia.princeton.edu/sites/default/files/content/Breza_Emily_Paper.pdf). The 10% wage-cut magnitude and the private/public contrast are thus correct; the "in private, in the home" framing corresponds to the paper's private treatment where the offer/wage is not observable to other workers.

The norm-based rationale is also documented: about 80% of workers say it is "unacceptable" or "very unacceptable" for an unemployed worker to offer to work below the prevailing wage (quoted from the paper in https://www.promarket.org/2020/05/21/indecent-proposals-in-economics-the-moral-problem-with-randomized-trial-experiments/), and workers pay to sanction anonymous laborers who accept wage cuts (37% of players choose to punish wage-cut acceptors; workers give up ~49% of average weekly earnings to avoid being seen breaking the norm) (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25880/revisions/w25880.rev3.pdf).

No factual error found; the numbers cited ("less than 2%" and "a quarter") are accurate renderings of 1.8% and 26%.
